a4003.speech: Maintains that Malawi’s economy continues to face significant challenges and that in order to create the conditions for growth, “there is a need to shift from business as usual” ; “The GDP growth forecast for 2025 has been downgraded to 2.0%, from 4.2% at the end of 2024, due to the impact of a weak agricultural season, continued foreign exchange shortages [that is] impeding the importation of production inputs — along with the suspension of some bilateral foreign assistance. The premature end of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) programme may also impact budget support and other external financing” ; projects that “real GDP growth is projected at 2.4% in 2026”, adding that “this stagnation impedes efforts to reduce poverty.”

a4003.speaker: World Bank (Malawi Economic Monitor, 21st edition, July 2025, ‘Navigating Uncertainty’)
a4003.speech: “Fiscal and external imbalances continue to deteriorate. The budget deficit is expected to remain high in FY2025/26, driven by election year spending and the need to absorb some critical expenditures previously financed by bilateral support. Inflation is expected to remain above 30% due to a weaker agricultural recovery, the imposition of new import bans constraining supply, as well as continued high money supply growth. If the official exchange rate remains overvalued, it will continue to incentivise imports and discourage export growth, deepening external imbalances. As elections approach, macro-fiscal risks are rising. Depleted buffers and persistent fiscal and current account deficits leave Malawi susceptible to external shocks and other crises. Continued delays in advancing reforms increases the risks of further deterioration. External conditions are also becoming increasingly less favorable as foreign aid flows continue declining and global policy uncertainty spills over into Malawi. Climate-related shocks are also becoming more severe and urgent. Elections create their own fiscal risks as spending and borrowing pressures intensify. However, Malawi’s recent history also provides lessons to policymakers on how severe macro-fiscal crises can be overcome.”

a4003.speaker: World Bank (Malawi Economic Monitor, 21st edition, July 2025, ‘Navigating Uncertainty’)
a4003.speech: Says that in the context of growing imbalances and increasing global challenges, it will be critical for the economy to become more resilient: “Currently the policy and institutional framework do not effectively support the adjustment of the economy to shocks. A fixed and overvalued exchange rate and highly pro-cyclical fiscal policy means that at the macroeconomic level, imbalances accumulate, and adjustment costs can be large and sudden. These are in turn often borne by the most vulnerable. At the household level, there are also numerous structural impediments to resilience that constrain entrepreneurship and the functioning of markets. Building more resilience into the economy means shifting towards a growth and development model that is adaptive and commensurate with Malawi’s state capacity and its revenues. Achieving this will require the government to focus its efforts on the most critical issues, where the public sector is best suited to lead.”

a4003.speaker: World Bank (Malawi Economic Monitor, 21st edition, July 2025, ‘Navigating Uncertainty’)
a4003.speech: “The outlook is subject to significant downside risks, including potential budgetary overruns, especially in the context of election spending pressures, that could further entrench macroeconomic instability. While direct and indirect effects of recent trade conflicts have caused a downward shift in growth projections, continued uncertainty and weaker-than-expected global demand may further adversely affect Malawi’s growth prospects. Climate-related disasters and failure to address external imbalances may further perpetuate input shortages. Upside risks include the easing of trade restrictions, faster-than-expected development of mining mega-projects, and the rapid conclusion of debt-restructuring negotiations with commercial external creditors.”

a4003.speaker: World Bank (Malawi Economic Monitor, 21st edition, July 2025, ‘Navigating Uncertainty’)
a4003.speech: Says key policy priorities include macroeconomic stability, increasing investment and exports, and resilience to shocks, and “argues for the importance of taking decisive actions to prevent a further deterioration of the economy — as Malawians navigate both global and domestic uncertainty”: “Malawi’s economy is facing increasing pressure from rising fiscal and external imbalances, shifting global trade and aid dynamics, and the upcoming general elections. When the new ‘homegrown strategy’ is announced, it is important that a focus on stabilisation is central — along with a coherent and consistent macroeconomic framework that does not further exacerbate fiscal and external imbalances.” Recommends urgent reforms in three areas: restoring macroeconomic stability (increasing domestic revenues, reducing wasteful spending, finalising debt restructuring and controlling borrowing, and reducing inflation by limiting money supply growth); supporting investment and export growth (phasing out the implicit fuel subsidy, implementing key mining sector reforms, phasing out foreign exchange surrender requirements and removing unnecessary trade barriers); and building resilience and protecting the poor (investing in climate-resilient agriculture, increasing the shock-responsiveness of the social protection system and importing grain for the coming lean season).

a4003.speaker: World Bank (Malawi Economic Monitor, 21st edition, July 2025, ‘Navigating Uncertainty’)
a4003.speech: Points out that there are “some bright spots in the economy that can drive growth over the medium term — especially through mega-projects in the energy and mining sectors”: “Critical decisions will need to be made in the coming months to ensure that these projects continue to advance and that the country can make the most of these opportunities.”

a4093.speaker: Trade union confederations CDTN and ITN (Niger)
a4093.speech: Through their speeches, reviewed the situation across the world, in Africa, in the sub-region and in Niger; in Niger, revisited the country’s new march towards its sovereignty and all the sacrifices that workers have consented to in order to support the new authorities in the face of the economic and financial sanctions imposed by the international community.

a4093.speaker: ITN (Niger trade union confederation)
a4093.speech: Put forward a number of grievances: the strengthening and intensification of patrols as part of securing people and their property; separating workers’ socio-professional organisations from other civil society structures in representations and bodies; and involving the trade union confederations more in matters of public interest, among others.

a4093.speaker: Workers (Maradi May Day participants)
a4093.speech: Reaffirmed their unwavering support for the struggle to improve the living and working conditions of their members.

a4093.speaker: Mamane Issoufou, Police Controller General, Governor of the Maradi region
a4093.speech: Recalled that on this date workers of the whole world pay tribute to their brothers and sisters who, in a peaceful gathering, obtained despite adversity the establishment of the 8-hour working day instead of 16 hours, and said the anniversary is a gathering of all to have a positive thought for the memory of the victims of the events in Chicago and other cities of the United States ; “The 1st of May is also a fitting occasion to evaluate the achievements made for the benefit of workers and to take stock of those that remain to be done.”

a4093.speaker: Mamane Issoufou, Police Controller General, Governor of the Maradi region
a4093.speech: Indicated that the highest authorities of Niger, under the leadership of President Abdourahamane Tiani and Prime Minister Mahamane Lamine Zeine, make the pursuit of the well-being of all socio-professional strata their true credo; that the Government has made social dialogue one of its priorities to manage and prevent conflicts; commended the trade union confederations for creating a peaceful climate; and declared: “To fight against unemployment and poverty, the current authorities are multiplying initiatives with a view to improving the living conditions of all households and promoting their fulfilment” ; promised appropriate responses to the grievances falling within his competence, with the others to be transmitted to the relevant parties.

a4161.speaker: Government of Malawi
a4161.speech: Has said it is reviewing sections of the Competition and Fair Trading Act to protect local small and medium enterprises (SMEs) against foreign traders, with some amendments expected to be tabled in Parliament next year.

a4161.speaker: Patrick Botha, spokesperson of the Ministry of Trade and Industry
a4161.speech: Said in an interview on Saturday that they are consulting to have a proposed list of businesses to be reserved to indigenous Malawians, saying in the absence of legislation, it would be difficult to regulate ; pointed out that Dapp Malawi, which sells kaunjika (second-hand clothes) both on retail and wholesale, has been asked to choose one of the two ; “Central Poultry Limited sells day-old chicks, chickens and feed on retail. The vendors found it monopolistic. The ministry reminded the company not to sell chickens to end consumers but to agents and distributors” ; revealed that some of the businesses the vendors have already listed include kaunjika, clearance of freight, groceries, transportation of goods, stand-alone bakeries and taxi services.

a4161.speaker: Gomezgani Nyasulu, Mzuzu City Council chief executive officer
a4161.speech: Said the reform seeks to preserve specific businesses and categories for indigenous Malawians and is ultimately expected to stop issuance of retail business licences to foreign traders ; said the next engagement, as council, will be with Malawi Police Service, to resolve issues of multitude ad hoc road blocks within the city and Malawi Defence Force on alleged harassment of vendors at Chilumba Roadblock in Karonga.

a4161.speaker: James Chiutsi, executive secretary of the Chamber for Small and Medium Businesses Association
a4161.speech: Said despite having a liberalised market, government can implement such reforms to give an opportunity for SMEs to thrive: “That is a positive development. We are aware that there are a lot of Malawians trading in the same businesses as the foreigners. We need to attract meaningful foreign investment only. Micro SMEs are in the largest numbers and are the most vulnerable even in the face of the smallest shocks. Protecting them is government’s duty.”

a4161.speaker: Tennyson Mulimbula, general secretary of the Small-Scale Business Operators Association of Malawi
a4161.speech: Said the review would promote the growth of businesses owned by indigenous traders who, he said, have been squeezed by foreign traders: “The Trade Act stipulates that a business license for foreign investors requires a minimum capital investment of $250 000 (K433 million) brought in from outside the country. Therefore, the nullification of issuance of retail business licences for foreign traders is 100 percent applicable.”

a4161.speaker: Alexander Sikwese, Mzuzu vendors overall chairperson
a4161.speech: Said in an interview that they are excited with the move but hoped that it would materialise.

a4317.speaker: National Health Institute (INS) of Mozambique (daily Covid-19 reports) and analyst Miguel de Brito
a4317.speech: Daily Covid-19 reports published by the INS, first published each afternoon by Miguel de Brito, are the source for the reported case and death figures (895 new cases and 8 deaths on 18 January; 8,313 active cases, 47% in Maputo).

a4317.speaker: Josep Borrell, EU High Representative/Foreign Minister
a4317.speech: Said last week that an EU mission was scheduled to arrive in Maputo tomorrow (19 Jan), but admitted the mission still does not have permission, and said he hopes the mission will go to Cabo Delgado if Mozambique permits ; stressed that any EU initiatives could only be developed after “the agreement of the authorities in Mozambican, which is a sovereign country”, and pointed to possible military training and equipment, humanitarian aid and coastal surveillance.

a4317.speaker: Human Rights Watch (World Report 2021)
a4317.speech: Says “State security forces were implicated in grave human rights violations … including arbitrary arrests, abductions, torture of detainees, excessive force against unarmed civilians, intimidation and extrajudicial executions. The government did not take any publicly known step to investigate those abuses or punish those implicated.”

a4317.speaker: Trump administration / Anthony Tata, “performing the duties of under secretary of defense for policy”
a4317.speech: Offered military training and equipment to Mozambique at a meeting in Maputo on 8 January with Minister of Defense Jaime Neto and Minister of Interior Amade Miquidade; Tata has called President Barack Obama a “terrorist leader” and has been a Fox News regular defending Trump.

a4317.speaker: USAID (new policy, 14 January)
a4317.speech: Rushed out a new policy saying that the top priority of USAID’s economic-growth programs will be to “Benefit the US economy and the American people”.

a4317.speaker: Control Risks (consultants, global risk maps)
a4317.speech: Consider Mozambique relatively low risk compared to other parts of the world; its Africa risk map treats Mozambique, South Africa and Tanzania as “medium” security and political risk except for eastern Cabo Delgado which is high security risk, and treats all of Mozambique as low maritime risk, by contrast with the coasts of Ghana, Nigeria and Kenya.

a4317.speaker: Julia Mwito, provincial director of Land, Environment and Rural Development (Gaza province)
a4317.speech: Told Noticias (21 Dec) that more than 140,000 hectares of land in Gaza allocated to commercial farmers is not being properly used and will be taken back by the state, and that in 92 cases investor plans are not being carried out so the DUATs will be cancelled.

a4317.speaker: Joao Mosca, director of the Rural Observatory and professor at Universidade Politecnica
a4317.speech: Asks how we explain that the same people have passed from socialists and defenders of a strong state “to weakening the state to facilitate the theft of natural resources and various forms of trafficking?” ; “Its ideological flip-flops were only short-term strategies, always keeping in mind the reproduction of the monopoly of power,” and offers a periodization: 1962-68 nationalism, 1968-76 populism, 1977-86 socialism, 1987-2010 neo-liberalism and free market, and 2011-20 “without ideology, savage capitalism, and looting”.

a4317.speaker: Antonio Francisco, research director of IESE and professor at UEM
a4317.speech: Takes a cynical and humorous look at the $2 bn secret debt and at former Finance Minister Manuel Chang, arguing that to illegally commit Mozambique to a $2 bn debt that was 17% of GDP he must have been a “sublime optimist” and believer in national myths, participating in a modern version of Robin Hood, stealing from the poorest country in the world to give to the rich – and themselves: “Are con-men and politicians the most optimistic?”

a4464.speaker: United States government under President Donald Trump
a4464.speech: Announced plans to close nearly 30 embassies and consulates worldwide, with over half of them located in Africa; the proposed closures aim to cut the State Department’s budget by nearly 50% and reduce foreign aid by approximately 75%.

a4613.speaker: Elon Musk, Tesla CEO and top advisor to President Trump
a4613.speech: Said the Wisconsin Supreme Court vote could determine “the future of civilization”; said he would pay supporters of the conservative candidate $20 for every voter they recruit for their cause in the next two days.

a4613.speaker: Elon Musk, Tesla CEO and top advisor to President Trump
a4613.speech: “And if the (Wisconsin) Supreme Court is able to redraw the districts, they will gerrymander the district and deprive Wisconsin of two seats on the Republican side,” he said at a rally in Green Bay on Sunday. “Then they will try to stop all the government reforms we are getting done for you, the American people.” ; “I think this will be important for the future of civilization. It's that significant.”

a4613.speaker: Josh Kaul, Wisconsin attorney general (Democrat)
a4613.speech: Made a bid to block Musk's giveaways on Sunday, but the state Supreme Court rejected his lawsuit minutes before Musk's rally kicked off.

a4613.speaker: Wisconsin Supreme Court (ruling)
a4613.speech: Rejected the attorney general's lawsuit seeking to block Musk's giveaways, minutes before Musk's rally kicked off; two lower courts had already rejected the legal challenge.

a4613.speaker: New York University's Brennan Center for Justice
a4613.speech: According to the Brennan Center, as of last week groups affiliated with Musk had spent at least $17.5 million to support Schimel.

a4933.speaker: Air Marshal Hasan Abubakar, Chief of the Air Staff, Nigerian Air Force / Chairman of the Association of African Air Forces
a4933.speech: emphasised the need for African-led solutions to the continent's security challenges; highlighted the importance of regional collaboration and strategic partnerships in strengthening African airpower capabilities and addressing common threats; stressed that enhanced cooperation among African Air Forces is crucial for tackling emerging security challenges such as terrorism, insurgency, and transnational crime; underscored the role of strategic partnerships with allied nations and international organisations in building capacity, enhancing interoperability, and advancing technological innovations in aerospace operations ; said the AAAF symposium is more than just a meeting of minds but a demonstration of commitment towards a safer, more secure, and more prosperous Africa: "Our collaboration is a powerful reminder of the importance of finding African solutions to African problems." ; called for renewed commitment from all member states, stressing that unity and cooperation remain critical to achieving the Association's objectives.

a4933.speaker: Nigerian Air Force press statement signed by Air Vice Marshal Olusola F Akinboyewa, Director Public Relations and Information, Headquarters NAF
a4933.speech: noted that the new AAAF Chairman outlined key priorities for his tenure, including the full operationalisation of the Association and the enhancement of Africa-led Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Response (HADR) operations, and that he assured members of Nigeria's commitment to delivering a successful African Air Chiefs' Symposium in 2026.

a5278.speaker: President Donald Trump and his adviser Elon Musk
a5278.speech: Have criticised USAID, arguing that overseas spending does not represent value for American taxpayers.

a5278.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a5278.speech: Has described senior USAID officials as "radical lunatics" and has long advocated for cutting foreign aid.

a5356.speaker: Zhao Jiang Ping, China's Ambassador to Burundi
a5356.speech: Said that this year sino-Burundian cooperation is undergoing an accelerated and general revival in all areas, looking back at President Evariste Ndayishimiye's recent visit to China: "The two countries signed the Letter of Creation of the sixth phase of the project to send high-level agricultural experts. The 22nd Chinese medical team in Burundi, made up of 29 members, has arrived in Burundi and has begun its mission" ; added that the team of the Chinese company carrying out the project to divert National Road No. 1 has arrived in Bujumbura for the initial preparations ; indicated that the two parties had reached a preliminary understanding on the Implementation Agreement for the rehabilitation, extension and modernisation of Melchior Ndadaye International Airport, "The project should officially begin as early as next year" ; indicated that in 2023 more than 200 Burundians travelled to China to take part in bilateral and multilateral seminars and training.

a5356.speaker: Zhao Jiang Ping, China's Ambassador to Burundi
a5356.speech: Emphasised that "Achieving common development and progress is the hope of the two Heads of State, Burundian and Chinese", and said this 60th anniversary of diplomatic relations should be taken as a new starting point for continuing to strengthen cooperation and working hand in hand to open a bright future for sino-Burundian relations.

a5356.speaker: Zhao Jiang Ping, China's Ambassador to Burundi
a5356.speech: Explained that the "Belt and Road" Initiative constitutes today the largest platform for international cooperation and the biggest global public cooperation project, and indicated that it has already generated more than 3,000 cooperation projects, created 420 thousand jobs in the countries served and lifted nearly 40 million people out of poverty.

a5356.speaker: Albert Shingiro, Ambassador and head of Burundian diplomacy (Foreign Minister)
a5356.speech: Declared that "The Chinese and Burundian peoples have good reason to celebrate this anniversary together in joy and jubilation. For Burundi and China have maintained, for 60 years, excellent bilateral relations of sincere friendship and pragmatic cooperation, based on shared values of solidarity, fraternity, trust and mutual respect" ; acknowledged that these relations have been strengthened and diversified notably through trade, the construction of state infrastructure, and cooperation in agriculture, energy, food security, health and education.

a5356.speaker: Albert Shingiro, Ambassador and head of Burundian diplomacy (Foreign Minister)
a5356.speech: Said Burundi is aware that China is a partner full of consideration and concerned with the development of the Burundian people: "Burundi is happy to continue to maintain cordial relations with China, a reliable bilateral partner at all times and through all trials, which has always stood alongside the Burundian people, in times of peace as in times of conflict" ; said he is confident that China will continue to accompany Burundi in achieving the development objectives of the National Development Plan 2018-2027 and its vision, "Burundi: an emerging country in 2040 and a developed country in 2060."

a5356.speaker: Albert Shingiro, Ambassador and head of Burundian diplomacy (Foreign Minister)
a5356.speech: Clarified: "Here the use of the word accompany has been measured. It means, implicitly, that Burundi is solely responsible for its own development; partners intervene only to accompany national efforts."

a5356.speaker: Albert Shingiro, Ambassador and head of Burundian diplomacy (Foreign Minister)
a5356.speech: Reiterated Burundi's attachment to the policy of one single and indivisible China, with Taiwan as an integral part.

a5541.speaker: George Jobe, Malawi Health Equity Network (MHEN) expert/leader
a5541.speech: Says what America has done in suspending aid for 90 days should be a lesson to Malawi: “What matters now is that government quickly finds ways of plugging the gap that has opened. America has given 90 days to review its aid and we do not know the outcome of those 90 days. That is why we should always be prepared.”

a5541.speaker: George Jobe, Malawi Health Equity Network (MHEN) expert/leader
a5541.speech: Says there is still hope because America has not announced that it is stopping aid altogether through other organisations such as the Global Fund, which also supports areas such as health.

a5541.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a5541.speech: Ordered that USAID, the government branch that provides aid to other countries, halt its operations until he is satisfied that the agency’s work aligns with his vision.

a5541.speaker: Health organisations (Malawi)
a5541.speech: Have been urging government to meet the target of allocating K15 out of every K100 in the national budget to the Ministry of Health, as countries agreed, so that the ministry has enough money to operate instead of depending heavily on aid from other countries.

a5541.speaker: Senior chiefs (collectively)
a5541.speech: Say they are worried that the suspension of the aid could affect many people and could lead to deaths among people currently on life-prolonging ARV drugs.

a5541.speaker: Senior Chief Salima, of Salima district
a5541.speech: Said many people, especially in the villages, depend on free health services including those on life-prolonging ARV drugs, and the suspension of the aid is a hardship for such people: “Since this has happened we are looking to government, because we know it cannot allow people to perish just because aid has stopped; as things stand, only those with money or the bosses have a chance of getting proper health care.”

a5541.speaker: Senior Chief Mwabulambia, of Chitipa
a5541.speech: Said that apart from the crisis that may arise from the lack of health aid, agricultural work is also at risk because many farming projects such as irrigation also depend on that same aid: “Here we have no grounds to complain, because that money is theirs. What we must do is gradually shed the dependent life while making a plan to rely on ourselves. For example, we can make things like fertiliser ourselves, the way our friends in Zambia are doing.”

a5541.speaker: Senior Chief Kawinga, of Machinga
a5541.speech: Said that if there were an opportunity to speak with the American government, the chiefs would ask for such a chance so that they could themselves explain how people in the villages benefit from that country’s aid, so that it may continue: “It is like a blade sharpened on both sides: farming activities are disrupted on one side while health is disrupted on the other — especially these matters to do with Aids frighten us a great deal, because many people could leave us.”

a5542.speaker: South African Medical Research Council (SAMRC) and Bhekisisa’s calculations (data)
a5542.speech: Numbers from the SAMRC and Bhekisisa’s calculations show that South Africa receives R6.65 billion — or $350 million — in annual funding from the US government’s National Institutes of Health when the totals of direct grants, subgrants and funding from network studies are added up.

a5542.speaker: Bhekisisa data team (analysis)
a5542.speech: Bhekisisa’s data team’s sums reveal that if South Africa loses all of its NIH funding, the country could lose 70% of its medical research capacity — yet it would make less than a 1% difference to the NIH budget in the US.

a5542.speaker: NIH memo leaked in March (document)
a5542.speech: An NIH memo leaked in March, on which Bhekisisa and the science journal Nature reported, instructed officers to hold “all [research] awards to entities located in South Africa” and listed SA as a “country of concern”, along with China.

a5542.speaker: Linda-Gail Bekker, head of the Desmond Tutu Health Foundation
a5542.speech: “Getting to that point is hard work.” ; “A grant is never just ‘given’: each application is reviewed by a panel of experts and only if they find the proposed project has merit and so will be worth investing in, will they award the money.” She adds that grant holders also have to pass a clean audit every year, done to US rules, to prove that they’re spending the funds responsibly, and explains that getting funding through a network study means a researcher who is part of a unit that runs clinical trials gets awarded money for a study.

a5542.speaker: Linda-Gail Bekker, head of the Desmond Tutu Health Foundation
a5542.speech: Says that although the lenacapavir clinical trials weren’t directly funded by NIH money, they were done at research sites of which many have grants from the US agency — and have had for years — and that this type of backing lays the foundation for future research, like setting up facilities, paying scientists’ salaries and training young researchers ; “Great science is done in collaboration with the US and if that stops, it will create a huge [research] gap.”

a5542.speaker: Ntobeko Ntusi, CEO of the South African Medical Research Council (SAMRC)
a5542.speech: Told Bhekisisa that “before January 20, there was a second portal of the NIH that hit that level of granular detail [amounts linked to subgrants], which has [since] been disabled”; explains that roughly $100 million of NIH funding is awarded to South African researchers through subgrants every year, about $50 million through direct awards to principal investigators, and a further $200 million or so sits in funding from network studies, bringing the total to around $350 million.

a5542.speaker: Ntobeko Ntusi, CEO of the South African Medical Research Council (SAMRC)
a5542.speech: Says that the US investment over decades, which has helped to build high-calibre research capacity in South Africa, should not be forgotten: “Seminal contributions from our scientists have been good not only for the country, but also for the world. At the same time, we should continue to express solidarity with our peers in the US, who are similarly affected as we are. Many of them are losing their jobs, have had their grants terminated and are feeling overwhelmed.” Yet the US “will remain a really important player in global health”, Ntusi says, and despite the current upheaval, there’s “an opportunity [for scientists] to reimagine their research operations”.

a5542.speaker: Pepfar figures obtained by the South African health department (data)
a5542.speech: Figures that the health department obtained from the US government’s Aids fund, Pepfar, show that Pepfar-supported HIV and TB implementation projects that the Trump administration defunded in February come to a total loss of R4.45 billion for this financial year.

a5542.speaker: Modelling study (cited)
a5542.speech: A modelling study shows that if South Africa were to roll out lenacapavir soon, it could stop enough new infections that Aids would practically end being a public health threat in the country by 2032.

a5542.speaker: NIH website (data)
a5542.speech: According to the agency’s website, 6% of the NIH’s total budget covers admin, building maintenance and other operational costs.

a5634.speaker: Somali officials
a5634.speech: Said diphtheria cases and deaths have risen sharply this year in Somalia, where the response has been curtailed by vaccine shortages and US aid cuts.

a5634.speaker: Hussein Abdukar Muhidin, general director of Somalia's National Institute of Health
a5634.speech: Said more than 1,600 cases, including 87 deaths, have been recorded, up from 838 cases and 56 deaths in all of 2024.

a5634.speaker: Deka Mohamed Ali, mother of four children who contracted diphtheria
a5634.speech: "My children got sick and I just stayed at home because I did not know it was diphtheria," she told Reuters from the bedside of her 3-year-old son Musa Abdullahi whose throat was swollen to the size of a lemon from the infection.

a5634.speaker: Ali Hajji Adam, Somali Health Minister
a5634.speech: Said the government had struggled to procure enough vaccines due to a global shortage and that US aid cuts were making it difficult to distribute the doses it had ; "The US aid cut terribly affected the health funds it used to provide to Somalia. Many health centers closed. Mobile vaccination teams that took vaccines to remote areas lost funding and now do not work."

a5634.speaker: Hussein Abdukar Muhidin, general director of Somalia's National Institute of Health
a5634.speech: Separately echoed the health minister's comments about the closures.

a5634.speaker: US government statistics
a5634.speech: According to US government statistics, overall US foreign assistance commitments to Somalia stand at $149 million for the fiscal year that ends on September 30, compared with $765 million in the previous fiscal year.

a5634.speaker: US State Department spokesperson
a5634.speech: "The United States continues to provide lifesaving foreign assistance in Somalia," said when asked about the impact of its aid cuts in the country ; "America is the most generous nation in the world, and we urge other nations to dramatically increase their humanitarian efforts."

a5634.speaker: Save the Children
a5634.speech: Said last month that the closure of hundreds of health clinics in Somalia this year due to foreign cuts has contributed to a doubling in the number of combined cases of diphtheria, measles, whooping cough, cholera and severe respiratory infections since mid-April.

a5634.speaker: Amnesty International
a5634.speech: Said that in 2024 Somalia's government allocated 4.8 percent of its budget to health, down from 8.5 percent the previous year.

a5634.speaker: Somali health ministry (non-response)
a5634.speech: The health ministry did not respond to a question about the criticism from doctors and human rights activists over its limited funding of the health sector. It has said it is planning to launch a vaccination drive but has not given details when.

a5695.speaker: Industry players (banking sector)
a5695.speech: have described the move as retrogressive.

a5695.speaker: Highly placed sources within the banking sector (anonymous)
a5695.speech: revealed Thursday that they received the verbal communication during a virtual meeting.

a5695.speaker: A commercial banking source (anonymous)
a5695.speech: confided in us that commercial banks were still deliberating on the way forward ; “We are meeting to discuss this matter. If necessary, we will issue formal communication,” the source said.

a5695.speaker: Mark Lungu, RBM spokesperson
a5695.speech: denied that the directive had been issued ; “The government cannot issue directives regarding private accounts,” Lungu said, before referring us to the Accountant General.

a5695.speaker: Accountant General of Malawi
a5695.speech: The AG was unavailable for comment when we went to press.

a5695.speaker: Thabo Chakaka Nyirenda, Attorney General of Malawi
a5695.speech: accused some of the country’s non-governmental organisations (NGOs) of engaging in illegal foreign currency trading, allegedly depriving the nation of crucial forex; in a letter addressed to the NGO Regulatory Authority, accused the NGOs of colluding with banks and private businesses to facilitate the movement of forex received from abroad, benefiting private traders; warned that, legally, banks should only transfer foreign currency to third parties after it has been deposited with them, not directly from the foreign currency accounts of individuals or institutions, such as NGOs; claimed that the government was missing out on benefits that could have been accrued had banks sold the forex legally; threatened legal action against the alleged malpractice and singled out some senior officials in the banking industry as culprits; claimed that his office had gathered evidence of collusion among the financial controllers of local and international NGOs, donor-funded projects and treasury departments within commercial banks.

a5695.speaker: Thabo Chakaka Nyirenda, Attorney General of Malawi
a5695.speech: criticised RBM for its purportedly inadequate enforcement of the Exchange Control Act in addressing the issue.

a5737.speaker: A limited number of Israelis (letter to Donald Trump)
a5737.speech: Recently wrote a letter to Trump pleading with him to stop the war — one indication of the weariness and shame at the war's lack of any measure.

a5737.speaker: Well-known scholars of international relations
a5737.speech: Criticism has repeatedly been voiced among them that America, which ought to be listened to in its capacity as a superpower patron, has instead become the party tuned by Israel.

a5737.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a5737.speech: Said no more than “what is happening to the Palestinians concerns us… we want peace to be made.”

a5737.speaker: Hamas
a5737.speech: On Ginbot 18, 2017 E.C. (late May 2025) Hamas was said to be willing to agree to a 60-day ceasefire proposal presented by the American side, conditioned on the release of the remaining hostages.

a5737.speaker: Government of Israel
a5737.speech: Responded that there will be no ceasefire unless Hamas exits its military role and Trump's plan is implemented; in short, Netanyahu told the Palestinians and the world flatly that he will not turn back without embittering the Palestinians through collective assault or uprooting and scattering them.

a5737.speaker: Israeli representative at the UN Security Council
a5737.speech: At the UN Security Council meeting of Ginbot 20, 2017 E.C. on aid delivery to the Palestinians, what he “heard” from a presentation of Palestinian agony delivered through tears was a speech fanning antisemitism.

a5737.speaker: US representative at the UN Security Council
a5737.speech: Expounded on Israel's right to defend itself, on Hamas having to be defeated, and on the full release of the hostages, but did not speak a single sentence about the Palestinians' inviolable right to live in peace in Gaza.

a5737.speaker: Getachew Reda, head of the Tigray Interim Administration
a5737.speech: His interview with Fana Television and his plan to establish a new party can be said to have been the beginning of a feast bringing together long-standing and newly arrived seekers of change.

a5737.speaker: Debretsion Gebremichael and colleagues (petition to the African Union)
a5737.speech: The petition they wrote to the African Union was the voice of a death-rattle spirit coming from inside the grave.

a5737.speaker: Ethiopian Reporter (editor's note)
a5737.speech: “From the Editor: we wish to state that the article reflects only the writer's viewpoint.”

a5874.speaker: Frans Kapofi, Minister of Defence and Veterans Affairs of Namibia
a5874.speech: Is satisfied with the achievement of Exercise Hanganee 2 in fostering interactions and cultural practises among Namibian and Botswana defence forces; said the exercise provided an opportunity to deepen the country's bilateral relations and added that the operation will strengthen military-to-military cooperation ; "Apart from issues related to military relations, this exercise contributed immensely to the wellbeing of the community through outreach programmes such as provisional health services, basic necessities, and cleaning campaigns, to mention but a few. It is now my single honour and privilege to declare Exercise Hanganee 2 officially closed."

a5874.speaker: Brigadier Anderson Matlho, Exercise Co-Director, Botswana Defence Force
a5874.speech: Acknowledged the commitment and dedication shown by officers of both countries during the exercise ; "If I didn't recognise and appreciate the hard work demonstrated by exercise planners to put this exercise together, it is always not easy to achieve maximum desirable results from people coming from different backgrounds, but we maintain the same spirit and work ethic as we came to conclude this exercise."

a5956.speaker: Human Rights Watch (statement)
a5956.speech: “The Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (GSIM), affiliated with Al-Qaeda, attacked the town of Djibo, in the Sahel region, on 11 May, and the village of Youba, in the northern region, on 3 August, killing at least 40 civilians” ; “The Islamic State in the Sahel (IS) attacked a civilian convoy delivering humanitarian aid to the besieged town of Gorom Gorom, in the Sahel region, on 28 July, killing at least nine civilians.”

a5956.speaker: Residents of the village of Youba
a5956.speech: Explained to HRW that the extremists wanted to “punish the local community for not having obeyed GSIM’s instructions to abandon certain crops.”

a5956.speaker: GSIM (Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims), in a response to HRW on 15 August
a5956.speech: Maintained that it had “never intentionally targeted civilians,” speaking of “unfounded allegations” or “at most, incidents caused by stray bullets,” of which it says it has no knowledge.

a5956.speaker: Ilaria Allegrozzi, Human Rights Watch Sahel researcher
a5956.speech: Considers that “the authorities must guarantee better protection for all civilians in danger.”

a5956.speaker: Captain Ibrahim Traore, head of the junta
a5956.speech: On taking power at the end of September 2022, promised to restore security within a few months.

a5956.speaker: Human Rights Watch
a5956.speech: Asks the authorities to “investigate the abuses, particularly those committed by the military and allied militias, and prosecute those responsible”; observes that “the Government has increasingly attacked civilians during” counterterrorism operations.

a5956.speaker: Acled (organisation that counts conflict victims worldwide)
a5956.speech: Reports more than 26,000 people killed in terrorist attacks — civilians and military — since 2015 in Burkina Faso, more than half of them in the last three years.

a6404.speaker: International Organisation for Migration (IOM)
a6404.speech: Has tipped Malawi to enhance collaboration to curb irregular migration, which is apparently rampant in the country but underreported.

a6404.speaker: Nomagugu Ncube, IOM Chief of Mission to Malawi
a6404.speech: Said surveys the organisation conducted recently revealed that irregular migration and trafficking in persons exist, but the figures it has are not a true reflection of what is on the ground, because the main means of operation by smugglers and traffickers is to avoid detection, hence the numbers are scanty: "I would say Malawi is doing well but it can do more in the sense that the government recognises there is an irregular migration challenge" ; "The second thing is to enhance collaboration among actors. For instance, the government is engaging the government of Mozambique to promote the use of a border pass so that people can move between the two countries regularly without using passports."

a6404.speaker: Nomagugu Ncube, IOM Chief of Mission to Malawi
a6404.speech: Also said IOM is aware of the issue of passports and urged the government to address it quickly so that it can facilitate regular migration.

a6404.speaker: Yoichi Oya, Japanese Ambassador to Malawi
a6404.speech: Hoped the vessel would enhance migration management around lakeshore districts: "Japan is a strong advocate for the concept of human security, emphasising the protection and empowerment of individuals and communities from various threats. This approach is deeply integrated into Japan's foreign policy and development assistance."

a6404.speaker: Fletcher Nyirenda, Commissioner responsible for Operations, Department of Immigration (Malawi)
a6404.speech: Acknowledged that their visibility was mostly on land and at airports, and said this gave smugglers and traffickers the chance to use the lake as an entry point without being detected: "So, we felt that our efforts were lacking because while we were doing well in other areas of border management, we have vast water bodies which include Lake Malawi and even the Shire River, which borders Mozambique. That is why we conceptualised this project and engaged our donor partners."

a6571.speaker: American Embassy in Namibia
a6571.speech: Said, of the Reach Namibia participant, "The 23-year-old chose the baking course and completed her internship at the Mello bakery with flying colours."

a6571.speaker: Dylan Maritz and Mike Samson, owners of the Mello bakery
a6571.speech: Give the programme staff important insights and information to ensure that the training courses correspond to the actual needs and conditions of the country's labour market.

a6571.speaker: Rosamunde, 23-year-old participant in the Reach Namibia project
a6571.speech: Describes herself as cheerful and happy, since she now has a job that helps to support her relatives at home by covering expenses such as food and hygiene products.

a6621.speaker: Pierre Simon Adovelande, National Coordinator of MCA-Benin
a6621.speech: At the opening of proceedings, provided all the necessary details through an exhaustive presentation of the work plan, under which about USD 225,090,677 will be invested in various activities of the MCA-Benin Programme from October to December 2008 across the four projects "Access to Land", "Access to Financial Services", "Access to Justice" and "Access to Markets". ; "This is the period when the great efforts and the great challenges get under way," the national Coordinator declared yesterday, adding that if the first and second years were used to launch the programme, it is now a matter of moving up to cruising speed. He thanked all the partners in this programme for the eminent role they play in it, and welcomed the commitment of the American side through the Millennium Challenge Corporation, which has helped to accelerate the activities already completed.

a6621.speaker: Pierre Simon Adovelande, National Coordinator of MCA-Benin
a6621.speech: "It is true that we have encountered some difficulties, but we have nonetheless come a long way. Our intervention, over 2 years, has brought many improvements in certain sectors of activity in the country, such as the Autonomous Port of Cotonou, which could have been downgraded a year ago without the support of MCA-Benin. There are also new practices and acquisitions of land titles that are under way. And between now and then, Beninese people will have the possibility of obtaining land titles for less than 200,000 CFA within a short time. In any case, we have a 5-year programme and we have just completed 2 years. We must not therefore expect immediate results. I ask the Beninese to be a little patient and they will be very proud and very happy to be beneficiaries of this programme by then."

a6621.speaker: Nestor Dako, Chairman of the Board of Directors of MCA-Benin
a6621.speech: Did not hide his joy and his deep gratitude regarding the various gains of this programme. "The coming year is a pivotal year and the year of the major achievements that will give greater visibility to the MCA-Benin Programme," he stressed. ; "The record is broadly positive after the two years that have passed and I am pleased about it. It is a record that deserves to be commended because it shows very important gains in the development of this programme. I am increasingly optimistic about its successful conclusion at the end of the three years that remain. I am all the more so because the rules that govern the actions within this programme remain very rigorous and are applied by men who are also very rigorous and very devoted to the task. There can therefore be no abuses, because everything is on a compact disc. Everything in it is locked down."

a6621.speaker: Sacca Fikara, Deputy and member of the Board of Directors of MCA-Benin
a6621.speech: "This programme is strongly supported by the National Assembly, which is putting all its means into playing its own part in its success. Organising the study of the codes in Parliament is a major concern of all the deputies and we are working to speed it up. Contrary to what is being said, the National Assembly is taking no action aimed at blocking the progress of this programme, because our activities are not limited solely to plenary sittings. There are internal committees working every day on this file without much noise. I want to reassure all the people, officials at various levels and the partners involved in this programme that the required codes will be adopted. I also thank the MCA for everything it is doing in Benin."

a6621.speaker: Patrick Noyes, Vice-President of the CCIB and member of the Board of Directors of MCA-Benin
a6621.speech: "It is necessary for the CCIB to contribute strongly to the success of the MCA-Benin programme. That is what we are trying to do, because many of our members are involved in it. We insist above all on land tenure, which is one of the important projects of this programme and which is the foundation of a good agricultural policy. In any case, Year 3, as I see it, will not be at all restful, because a great deal of investment will become effective. This is very good news for all Beninese."

a6684.speaker: United States Embassy (statement)
a6684.speech: Communicated that all persons who intend to apply for one of these visas must change the privacy settings of their social media accounts to "public" mode; according to the Embassy's statement, the measure aims to facilitate the verification processes necessary to establish the identity and admissibility of applicants to North American territory, as provided for in US legislation.

a6731.speaker: US Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), publication of 15 February
a6731.speech: announcing the cancellation of a $14 million grant (about 8.8 billion CFA francs) originally intended to support social cohesion in Mali.

a6731.speaker: Government of Mali
a6731.speech: expressed its surprise and indignation following the publication, on 15 February, by the United States Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), announcing the cancellation of a $14 million grant.

a6731.speaker: Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation of Mali (communique of 24 February 2025)
a6731.speech: sought to clarify the country's position on this matter and to denounce once again the use of official development assistance as an “instrument of destabilisation” ; The government states it has “approached the American authorities” to obtain explanations for the cancellation of this grant ; Bamako denounces a broader practice, which it considers to be an “attempt to instrumentalise public aid in order to weaken the sovereignty of African states”.

a6731.speaker: Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation of Mali (communique of 24 February 2025)
a6731.speech: recalls that “well before the installation of the new American administration, Mali was already sounding the alarm about these abuses”, which, according to the Transition authorities, serve in particular to “finance terrorist networks operating in the Sahel”.

a6731.speaker: Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation of Mali (communique of 24 February 2025)
a6731.speech: calls on Washington to bring legal proceedings against those responsible for these misappropriations of funds; according to the Malian authorities, sums intended for the country's development were “diverted for subversive purposes contrary to the essential needs of the population.”

a6731.speaker: Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation of Mali (communique of 24 February 2025)
a6731.speech: stresses that “Mali recognises itself in the new orientation of the American authorities aimed at cleaning up and humanising their grants”, while insisting on the need to “prevent any abusive use, or use contrary to the interest of recipient states.”

a6731.speaker: Government of Mali
a6731.speech: demands that “all cooperation respect the country's sovereignty and the priorities defined by the State” ; reaffirms its commitment to peace and stability, specifying that international cooperation must take place on “the basis of mutual respect and reciprocal interests” ; “Any future cooperation must respect the sovereignty of the Malian State and respond to the real expectations of the people.”

a6731.speaker: President of the Transition of Mali
a6731.speech: has made “the restoration of national sovereignty a fundamental principle of governance.”

a7204.speaker: Bank of South Sudan (statement signed by Governor Dr Addis Ababa Othow)
a7204.speech: Announced it had lowered the central bank lending rate to commercial banks by 200 percentage points after a unanimous decision by the Monetary Policy Committee: "To achieve these measures, MPC revised key policy instruments and unanimously agreed to reduce the central bank rate by 200 percentage points from 15 percent to 13 percent, spur and stimulate credit to the private sector and support robust economic growth." ; "The MPC maintained the Reserve Requirement Ratio (RRC) for South Sudan Pound (SSP) at 20 percent of total deposits and raised the RRR for foreign currency (e.g. US dollars, Euro or Sterling Pound) from 20 percent to 25 percent of total deposits with immediate effect." ; "The Bank of South Sudan remains committed to supporting the economy at these tough times, and we are confident the bank sector will navigate successfully through fears and uncertainty."

a7204.speaker: Johny Ohisa Damian, then Central Bank Governor of South Sudan
a7204.speech: Said the move to lift the SSP 10 million cash withdrawal limit for individual accounts was intended to encourage savings by prompting commercial banks to offer interest on savings accounts.

a7283.speaker: PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) audit report on ECG's books for the 3rd quarter of 2024
a7283.speech: "We found that the collection amounts in the CWM were lower than those in the ECG Cash Settlement Platform Report. The CWM recorded an amount of GH¢2.72 billion, while the ECG Cash Settlement Platform Report for the Task 1 period showed GH¢3.29 billion. In summary, the discrepancies between the CWM and the amounts in the ECG Cash Settlement Platform Report are as follows: October 2023: GH¢404,816,039; November 2023: GH¢104,768,729; December 2023: GH¢57,948,229" ; "For the three-month period from October to December 2023, the total revenue collections in the CWM amounted to GH¢2.72 billion, whereas the monthly revenue collections reported in the ECG Revenue Collections Sheet for the same period totalled GH¢3.33 billion. Significantly, there were discrepancies in both the total collection amounts and the reconciliations between tariff and non-tariff collections" ; also found that the total revenue in the CWM was GH¢1.14 billion less than the total amount of money in the company's bank statements, and revealed that ECG maintained 84 bank accounts with 20 different banks, despite a directive to consolidate all revenue collections and disbursements into a single account.

a7283.speaker: President John Mahama
a7283.speech: Directed that the persistent mismanagement issues plaguing the utility company be addressed, a directive followed by the Energy Minister's inauguration of a seven-member committee tasked with exploring private sector participation in ECG.

a7405.speaker: Jess Long, US embassy chargé d’affaires
a7405.speech: “The DREAMS programme aims to prevent HIV infection in adolescents and young women aged 10 to 24 years. The programme will continue to grow in 2022, and will reach 80 000 adolescent girls and young women with HIV prevention interventions.”

a7405.speaker: Jess Long, US embassy chargé d’affaires
a7405.speech: Added that additional activities included in the 2022 investment are support for recency testing, which is a procedure that shows the healthcare worker how recently a person was infected with HIV.

a7405.speaker: Jess Long, US embassy chargé d’affaires
a7405.speech: “Namibia has made strides in the fight against HIV, and is a global leader in nearing epidemic control. PEPFAR supports several different interventions that will bring Namibia closer to epidemic control and strengthen Namibia’s healthcare system.”

a7510.speaker: Seasoned delegates and veterans of countless communiqués (Africa Climate Summit)
a7510.speech: Muttered that the carnival of panels and photo-ops felt eerily familiar.

a7510.speaker: A growing band of activists
a7510.speech: Reject both the charity model and market-based fixes, instead advancing alternatives grounded in justice and systemic reform. To them, modern climate finance reeks of "carbon colonialism". They accuse African negotiators of a "sell-out" for flirting with carbon markets and denounce "extractive colonialism", in which African territories are sliced up for external speculators. They place the problem in what they label "kleptocratic capitalism", a global system built on primitive accumulation and dispossession. ; Argue that the industrial North owes Africa a "climate debt" not only for historic emissions but also for having strait-jacketed the continent's development, and that reparations, not loans and compensation, should sit at the centre of any settlement; that debt, carbon markets and "green" funds intersect to keep Africa subordinate.

a7510.speaker: Thabo Mbeki, former South African President
a7510.speech: Talk of an "African Renaissance" pushed debate beyond plaintive appeals; his old demand was for quality governance and African ownership.

a7510.speaker: Many African technocrats
a7510.speech: Prefer to sharpen the tools at hand, negotiating softer terms within today's system while still courting commercial capital. What matters, they insist, is not the label on the instrument but its cost and the control it confers. They believe Africa's agency is greater than the grievance narrative presents. The prudent path, many say, is to reform the system from within while exploiting every lever available.
